8.1.crux: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at thin cork through a microscope and saw tiny boxes. He called them cells.

cards.title: Too small to see
say: Most cells are far too small to see with our eyes alone.
To see them we need a microscope, which makes tiny things look much bigger.

cards.title: A microscope

labels.name: Mirror
labels.note: Throws light up through the sample

say: Light passes up through a very thin sample.
The lenses make it look many times bigger.
cards.remember: The sample must be thin so light can pass through it.

cards.title: Hooke's cork

labels.name: Thin slice of cork
labels.note: Cork is part of the bark of a tree

say: In 1665 Robert Hooke cut a thin slice of cork and looked at it under his microscope.
He saw many small boxes side by side, like a honeycomb.
He called each box a cell. 'Cell' means a small room.

cards.title: Discovery timeline

steps.text: 1665: Robert Hooke sees boxes in cork and names them cells.
Better microscopes are made over the next 150 years.
Scientists see that all living things are made of cells.

say: Hooke's cork cells were dead: only their walls were left.
Later, better microscopes let scientists study living cells.
cards.think: Why did learning more about cells have to wait for better microscopes?

crux_points: Cells are too small to see without a microscope.
Robert Hooke saw cells in a thin slice of cork in 1665.
He named them cells because they looked like small rooms.

quiz.q: What did Robert Hooke look at when he saw cells?
quiz.why: Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork, part of the bark of a tree.

quiz.q: Which part of the microscope is marked with '?'
quiz.why: The eyepiece is at the top: it is where you put your eye.

8.2.crux: Every living thing is built from cells, just as a building is built from bricks.

cards.title: Bricks of life

items.sub: The brick is the smallest building block
The cell is the smallest living block

say: A building is made of bricks joined together.
In the same way, the body of every living thing is made of cells.
cards.remember: The cell is the basic structural unit of life.

cards.title: Everything alive has cells
say: Plants, animals, people and tiny microbes are all made of cells.
Some living things have only one cell. Others have a huge number.

cards.title: One egg, one cell

items.sub: A single cell you can see without a microscope
The biggest single cell: about 17 cm long

say: Not every cell is tiny. A hen's egg is one single cell.
The ostrich egg is the largest cell known.
cards.think: If an egg is one cell, why can we see it without a microscope?

cards.title: Cells work together

steps.text: Tissue: a group of similar cells doing one job.
Organ: different tissues working together, like the heart.
Organism: all the organs together make a living body.

say: Cells join to form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs make up the whole body.

crux_points: All living things are made of cells.
The cell is the basic unit of life, like a brick in a building.
Cells can be tiny or, like an egg, big enough to see.

quiz.q: Why do we call the cell the 'basic unit' of living things?
options: All living things are built from cells
quiz.why: Every living thing is built up from cells, the way a wall is built from bricks.

quiz.q: Which of these is a single cell?
quiz.why: An egg is one single cell. A leaf, a heart and a tree are made of many cells.

8.3.crux: Some living things are just one cell, others have many; cells come in many shapes and sizes to suit their jobs.

cards.title: One cell or many?

cols.head: Unicellular
cells: That one cell does every job

say: 'Uni' means one and 'multi' means many.
A single-celled organism eats, breathes, grows and reproduces with just one cell.

cards.title: Shapes of cells

labels.name: Amoeba
labels.note: One cell with no fixed shape

say: Cells have different shapes because they do different jobs.
A nerve cell is long and branched so it can pass messages over long distances.
cards.remember: The shape of a cell suits the job it does.

cards.title: Amoeba's false feet

steps.text: Amoeba pushes out a finger-like bulge called a pseudopodium (false foot).
The bulge helps it move along.
Bulges also wrap around food and take it in.

say: An amoeba keeps changing its shape.
These changing bulges help it move and catch food.

cards.title: Sizes of cells

steps.text: Smallest: bacteria, only 0.1 to 0.5 micrometre across
Most cells in our body: need a microscope to see
A hen's egg: one cell you can hold in your hand
Largest: the ostrich egg, about 17 cm long

say: The smallest cells, like bacteria, are less than a micrometre across.
A micrometre (µm) is one-millionth of a metre.
cards.remember: The size of a cell has nothing to do with the size of the animal: an elephant's cells are not bigger than a mouse's.

crux_points: Unicellular organisms have one cell; multicellular organisms have many.
Cells have different shapes because they do different jobs.
Cell size does not depend on how big the animal is.

quiz.why: Amoeba is a single cell that does every job by itself.
It is long with many branches: a nerve cell, built to carry messages.

quiz.q: Are an elephant's cells bigger than a mouse's cells?
options: No, they are about the same size
quiz.why: Bigger animals have more cells, not bigger ones.

8.4.crux: A cell's shape and parts suit its job; similar cells form tissues, and tissues form organs.

cards.title: Built for the job

cols.head: Muscle cell
cells: Shortens and stretches to move body parts

cols.head: Blood cell
cells: Moves in blood, carries oxygen or fights germs

say: Each kind of cell has a shape that helps it do its job well.

cards.title: From cell to body

steps.text: Muscle tissue (many similar muscle cells together)
Heart: an organ made of muscle and other tissues
The body: many organs working together

say: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job.
An organ, like the stomach or the heart, is made of different tissues working together.

cards.title: Teamwork in the body

items.sub: Nerve tissue sends and receives messages

say: Plants have tissues and organs too: a leaf is a plant organ.
Every organ has a job, and its tissues are made of cells suited to that job.

crux_points: A cell's shape suits the job it does.
A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job.
Organs are made of tissues; organs together make the organism.

options: A group of similar cells doing one job
quiz.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together on one job.

quiz.q: Why are nerve cells long and branched?
options: To carry messages over long distances
quiz.why: Their long branches reach far, so messages can travel through the body.

8.5.crux: Every cell has three basic parts: a cell membrane outside, jelly-like cytoplasm inside, and a nucleus that controls the cell.

cards.title: Three basic parts
say: Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
Each part has its own job, like rooms in a house.

cards.title: Cell membrane: the gatekeeper
say: The cell membrane is a thin, porous cover around the cell.
It lets useful things in and waste out, and keeps the cell separate from its neighbours.
cards.remember: Plant cells also have a cell wall outside the membrane for extra strength.

cards.title: The nucleus: control centre
say: The nucleus is usually round and near the middle of the cell.
It holds chromosomes, which carry genes.
Genes pass features like eye colour from parents to children.

cards.title: Cytoplasm and its tiny parts

items.sub: Jelly between the membrane and the nucleus
A store; small in animal cells, large in plant cells
Green plastids in plant cells that make food using sunlight

say: Cytoplasm fills the cell and holds many tiny parts called organelles.
Cytoplasm and nucleus together are called protoplasm, the living part of the cell.

cards.title: Cells without a proper nucleus
say: In bacteria the nucleus has no membrane around it.
Cells like these are called prokaryotic cells.

crux_points: Cell membrane: the cover that controls what goes in and out.
Cytoplasm: the jelly that holds the cell's tiny parts.
Nucleus: the control centre with chromosomes and genes.

quiz.why: The round body in the middle is the nucleus, the control centre.

quiz.q: What carries the genes that pass features from parents to children?
quiz.why: Chromosomes in the nucleus carry genes.

quiz.q: Bacteria have no nuclear membrane. They are called…
quiz.why: Cells without a nuclear membrane are prokaryotic.

8.6.crux: Plant and animal cells share a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus, but only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a big vacuole.

cards.title: A plant cell

labels.name: Large vacuole
labels.note: A big store of water and food

say: A plant cell is often box-shaped because of its stiff cell wall.
A big vacuole fills much of the middle.

cards.title: An animal cell
say: An animal cell has no cell wall, so its shape is not fixed.
Its vacuoles are small, and it has no chloroplasts.

cards.title: Spot the difference
say: Both have a membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus.
The cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole belong only to plant cells.

cards.title: Why plants need a cell wall

items.sub: The wall protects against changes in temperature

say: Plants can't move to escape bad weather.
The extra wall gives each cell shape, strength and protection.

crux_points: Both cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.
Only plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.
Plant cells have one large vacuole; animal cells have small ones.

quiz.q: Which part is marked with '?' in this plant cell?
quiz.why: The small green bodies are chloroplasts, which make food using sunlight.

quiz.q: Which part is found ONLY in plant cells?
quiz.why: Animal cells have no cell wall.
Plant cells usually have one large vacuole; animal cells have small ones.
